title: Inspired sayings
hookLine: short verses the Buddha spoke from joy, each with its story

cards: Some things you say on purpose. Others just come out. You round a bend on a hike and the whole valley opens, and before you've decided anything you've said, oh.
A friend tells you good news and you laugh out loud. Those words aren't planned. They're breathed out.
The early Buddhist canon has a whole book built from moments like that: times when something happened, the Buddha saw what it meant, and a few lines of verse came out of him.
The book takes its name from that breathing out.

teach.b: Tradition explains udana as a breathing out, and the word means a heartfelt utterance, words spoken from a full heart, often from joy.
The book is part of the Khuddaka Nikaya, the collection of short books, alongside the Dhammapada and the Sutta Nipata you've just finished.
It has eighty discourses, in eight chapters of ten, and every one follows the same shape, which makes it easy to read.

teach.h: FIRST THE STORY, THEN THE VERSE.
teach.b: First, a short story in prose: where the Buddha was, who came, what happened. Then a formula, repeated eighty times: knowing the meaning of this, the Buddha, on that occasion, spoke this inspired saying. Then the verse.
The story is the soil and the verse is what grows from it.

The stories are often small and human: a woman in a long, hard labor; a monk homesick for his bride; boys at a pond; moths at a lamp. A few hold teachings this path will spend whole days on, starting tomorrow.
One more thing. Not every udana is joyful in the everyday sense.
Some come from sorrow, some from seeing something hard. But in every one, the verse comes after the Buddha sees what the moment means.

how: The Udana is read and taught in Theravada communities, and its verses are sometimes chanted.

o: a formal sermon to a large crowd
a chant recited before every meal
words breathed out from a full heart

p: the story: where, who, what happened

s: each udana has a short story and then a verse
the prose tells what happened; then the Buddha, seeing its meaning, speaks the verse.
the Udana is one long sermon
it's eighty short discourses in eight chapters of ten.
every udana comes from cheerful events

games.q: in the Udana, something has just happened in front of the Buddha. what usually comes next?
o: a long explanation to the monks.
knowing its meaning, he speaks a short verse.
games.why: the same formula appears eighty times: knowing the meaning of this, on that occasion he spoke this inspired saying.

practice: Think back over the past week for a moment that made you breathe out: a sky, a kindness, a child saying something unexpected.
Let the scene come back, the place and the light, and notice what it meant to you, with no need for words. Then let the breath go out slowly, the way it did then.

carryVoice: Your line: spoken from joy. Some of the truest words aren't planned. See you tomorrow.
